member.summary:
Module-Design.md names IOutboxWriter as one of the Infrastructure module's four public interfaces. This is that port: the only supported way for a business module to say "this happened, and something outside the request must eventually observe it".
Does not save. Like , the implementation adds rows to the caller's own unit of work and leaves the commit to the caller — which is precisely what makes ADR-0013's guarantee hold: the business state change and the Outbox row land in one transaction, or neither lands. A caller that rolls back leaves no Outbox message behind, so a rolled-back operation cannot notify anybody.
Nothing is sent from here. NFR-REL-01: nothing is dispatched from application code inside a request handler. Delivery is the Hangfire dispatcher's job (ADR-0015), after the transaction commits.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Authorization.AuthorizationGate
member.summary:
The single point through which every application-layer authorization decision in this solution is evaluated, and the one place the is applied to them (ADR-0024 — a confirmed management decision superseding Solution-Analysis.md §4.1's previous exclusion of System Administrator from operational actions).
Why a second mechanism exists at all. Authorization in Tiger CS Ticketing is enforced at two levels, by design: the ASP.NET Core policy catalog (ADR-0005) decides whether a caller may reach an endpoint, and the application services decide the resource-scoped part the policy cannot see — whether this caller may act on this ticket, given its current department and owner (Security-Architecture.md §3: "evaluated against the ticket's current data, not cached or assumed from the user's session alone"). SystemAdministratorOverrideHandler covers the first level for every present and future policy; this gate covers the second for every present and future application service. Together they are the "one central authorization mechanism" of the correction's requirement 4 — the override role itself is defined once, in , and neither level names it inline.
Usage rule. An application service must not branch on the override itself. It passes its own resource-scoped rule to / and uses the answer; the override is applied here, before the rule is consulted (and, for the async overload, without running it — an overridden caller costs no department-membership round trip). A new application service written this way includes the override automatically, which is exactly the property requirement 4 asks for.
What this gate is not. It decides permission only. Everything a service checks that is not a permission — request validation, ticket status-transition rules, closed-ticket immutability, optimistic concurrency, required business data, audit writes — sits outside the gate and is reached unchanged by an overridden caller. Per-record verification-session ownership (MVP-ERD.md §2.24) is deliberately outside it too; see ADR-0024's "Business rules the override does not reach".

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.CustomerVerification.CrmIntegration.ICrmBuyerLookupGateway
member.summary:
Tiger CRM's real, manually-verified GET /TicketingSystem/GetBuyerByPhone endpoint — a second, narrow read-only CRM port alongside (unit-number lookup) and ICrmCustomerLookupGateway (generic CRM/PACT/Tasleeh phone enrichment). This one is Buyer-specific: it returns every matching CRM customer plus the units each owns whose Lead is Sold or Contract, exactly as Tiger CRM itself already filters (MVP-Implementation-Backlog.md's CRM Buyer Lookup increment).
Read-only, and never resolves ambiguity on its own. This is the raw CRM contract boundary — it returns CRM's response exactly as CRM sent it, including the (expected-never-to-happen) case of more than one customer entry for one phone number. Business rule: CRM guarantees a phone number belongs to exactly one customer; enforcing/consolidating that (and staying resilient if CRM's own response does not honor it) is CrmBuyerLookupAppService's job, not this port's — this interface stays a thin, unopinionated passthrough. One customer may still own multiple valid units, and this port picks none of them: no automatic unit selection, matching the business rule that only the CS agent (via the New Ticket UI) may choose the relevant unit. This interface holds no verification state and makes no ticket-creation decision, matching every other CRM port's own documented boundary.
Implemented in TigerCS.Integrations.Modules.CrmIntegration (CrmBuyerHttpGateway) as a real HTTP-backed gateway — unlike /ICrmCustomerLookupGateway, no Mock implementation exists for this port: the CRM endpoint it calls has already been implemented and manually verified CRM-side, so this is a genuine integration from the start.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.CustomerVerification.CrmIntegration.ICrmGateway
member.summary:
The Tiger Group CRM's entire responsibility toward this system, and the only thing this interface may ever grow to do: read-only data access. Tiger CRM (i) looks up a unit by unit number, (ii) returns that unit's immutable CRM-issued identifier plus the minimum display details needed for an agent's verbal read-back, and (iii) returns the contacts/owners/tenants/authorized representatives linked to that unit. Nothing more.
This is a data-access integration port, not a verification authority. It holds no state machine, no session concept, no eligibility rule, no audit trail, and makes no decision about whether a ticket may be created — those are all Tiger CS Ticketing's own business logic (VerificationSessionAppService: selecting the requester, recording the verification method/result, deciding whether ticket creation is allowed, capturing the immutable verification-time snapshot, and the audit/authorization/expiry rules around all of it).
is this port's only caller — it does cache-aside lookups against this interface and nothing else; it is not where verification decisions are made either.
Implemented in TigerCS.Integrations.Modules.CrmIntegration — either a real HTTP-backed gateway, or the feature-flagged mock adapter used while real CRM endpoint details are unavailable (never described as production-ready — see MockCrmGateway). Any future automated intake surface (e.g. a Genesys AI voice/chat integration) that needs a unit or contact looked up must call Tiger CS Ticketing's own API — it must never call this interface, or any CRM system, directly: verification rules and the decision of whether a ticket may be created live only in Tiger CS Ticketing, and only Tiger CS Ticketing is a legitimate caller of a CRM data source.

member.summary:
Business-rule change: customer lookup is enrichment/identification, not a Ticket creation gate. Each of the three external sources — Tiger CRM, PACT, and Tasleeh — gets its own narrow, read-only, phone-search-only port, deliberately separate from ICrmGateway (that interface's own remarks scope it to unit-number lookup only; phone-based customer search is a different capability with a different caller, CustomerLookupAppService, and must never be able to widen ICrmGateway's own documented boundary).
Every implementation must fail closed, never block. A source that cannot be reached throws its own *GatewayUnavailableException (or, for PACT's outcome-wrapped port, returns a non-Success outcome); CustomerLookupAppService handles each source independently so one source's outage never affects another's result, and none of the three ever prevents a ticket from being created.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.CustomerVerification.PactIntegration.IPactCustomerLookupGateway
member.summary:
PACT's real customer/contract lookup by mobile number — the PACT counterpart of , and the port CustomerLookupAppService's PACT leg searches when a Department's DepartmentCustomerLookupSource configuration enables the Pact source. Backed by PACT's GET v1/contracts/{mobile} (the customer's contracts/units) and GET v1/contracts/{mobile}/customer-type (the customer's PACT-recorded type, fetched only when the contracts response did not already carry one).
Read-only, and never resolves ambiguity on its own. Returns every matched customer (0..N) with every contract/unit PACT associates with them (0..N) — no automatic selection of a first result, matching the business rule that only the CS agent may choose the relevant customer/ unit. PACT has no local UnitReference/ContactReference cache table, so a PACT contract is display enrichment for the agent, never linked to a Ticket by id.
Every failure mode maps to a outcome — implementations never throw for an expected PACT response (mirrors 's own contract): PACT being down, misconfigured, or answering garbage all collapse to a non-Success outcome, which CustomerLookupAppService reports as a Failed source alongside the other sources' results — a PACT failure or empty answer never blocks New Ticket creation, and the agent can always fall back to manual customer/unit entry.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.CustomerVerification.Services.CrmBuyerLookupAppService
member.summary:
The only caller of — searches Tiger CRM by phone number for Buyer records. CRM's own endpoint is the source of truth for which units are Sold/Contract-eligible: real CRM Lead status codes are not a small, stable, closed set Ticketing can safely hard-code (e.g. status 4 = "Contract" in production, not just 8/9 as an earlier, pre-launch assumption had it), so this service does not re-filter by at all — whatever CRM returns as a match, Ticketing accepts. The one check retained is 's CustomerType == Buyer: this phase supports Buyer matches only, and that is a Ticketing-side scoping decision, not a guess at CRM's own status semantics.
Business rule: a CRM phone number belongs to exactly one customer. CRM guarantees phone-number uniqueness per customer, so this service always resolves to at most one — never a list of distinct customers for the caller to disambiguate. A customer may still own multiple valid units, and every one of them is returned, unfiltered beyond the Buyer check above. A customer left with zero valid units after filtering is dropped entirely; a lookup left with zero customers after that becomes , even though CRM itself answered .
Never guesses when CRM breaks its own uniqueness guarantee. CRM naming the same CustomerId more than once is not a distinct-customer situation — merges those entries' units (deduplicated by UnitId) into one . But CRM naming two or more genuinely different CustomerIds for the same phone number is a real data-integrity conflict this service refuses to paper over: it does not pick a "first" customer, does not return a result at all, and never lets a Ticket or IntakeRecord get linked to either candidate automatically. Instead it returns and logs one warning for investigation — the phone number masked and the distinct CustomerIds named, but never CRM's secret key (this service never has it in the first place; see CrmBuyerHttpGateway). This service never throws for this case either.
No local reference/cache table exists for Buyer matches (see 's remarks) — this phase does not copy CRM master data into Ticketing; a future ticket-creation flow stores only the CRM identifiers plus an immutable ticket-time snapshot, not a synchronized copy of CRM's own customer/unit tables.

member.summary:
The integration boundary for Genesys-provided interaction context (Workflow/Automation phase 2). This DTO is the contract Ticketing needs — the fields Genesys is expected to hand over once an interaction is routed — deliberately defined here, on Ticketing's side of the boundary, because the exact Genesys API contracts are not finalized: nothing in this type assumes an endpoint shape, an auth model, or a payload encoding, and no Genesys API client exists in this phase.
Everything except the conversation id is optional, because Genesys' guarantees per channel are not confirmed — absent values are stored as null, never guessed. Interaction routing itself (Called Number → Queue, queue selection, agent selection) stays entirely inside Genesys; Ticketing persists this context verbatim for audit/traceability (TicketInteractionContext) and never re-derives routing from it.
Expected to be provided by Genesys later (per the operational design; to be confirmed with the finalized integration contract): channel, customer phone, called/destination number, queue id+name, agent id+name, conversation/interaction id, interaction start time, and direction where available. The customer phone still arrives through the existing intake (it is the verification identity input); when Genesys also supplies it, the intake value remains authoritative for verification. A future reverse direction (Ticketing → Genesys: ticket number/id, department, request type, status) is out of scope and only noted so this boundary stays extensible.

member.summary:
Decides where — if anywhere — a ticket's automated acknowledgement may be sent.
The verified snapshot is the only source, and this is a hard rule. ADR-0006 makes the CRM the sole source of truth for contacts and ADR-0007 freezes what the requester actually confirmed into TicketRequesterSnapshots at verification time. This resolver reads that row and nothing else: it never calls the CRM, never reads the ContactReferences cache (which is refreshable and may have changed since verification), and never writes any CRM-owned data. A ticket whose requester was verified in March is acknowledged at the address confirmed in March, which is the whole point of an immutable snapshot.
Nothing is ever guessed. There is no fallback to the creating agent, to a department mailbox, or to any staff address. Sending a customer's ticket details to a substituted recipient would be a disclosure incident, and no merged document authorises one.
Reported gap — no approved email column exists (CRITICAL). FR-NOT-01 requires an email acknowledgement and MVP-Data-Dictionary.md §2.21 provides RecipientAddress nvarchar(320) to hold the address, but §2.8's snapshot carries only SnapshotContactChannel, which Internal-CRM-API-Contract.md §5 defines as "the phone/email on file for this contact — used to cross-check that the caller matches CRM's own record": one free-text field, no type discriminator, cached for identity verification rather than for delivery. MVP intake is phone-only, so the common value is a phone number. No merged document says which field to send to, or what to do when the value is not an address.
Rather than invent a rule, this resolver accepts the channel value only when it is already a syntactically valid email address and reports otherwise. That outcome is a recorded, dead-lettered, audited, operator-visible fact — not a silent skip and not a guess. A business decision is required on where a requester's email address comes from.

Renders the FR-NOT-01 acknowledgement body.
Approved fields only, and the list is shorter than either source asks for — deliberately. FR-NOT-01 specifies "ticket number, expected response time, assigned department, and Geyness reference". Two of those four could not be honoured as written, and neither gap was papered over:
"Geyness reference" is omitted (HIGH, reported). ISSUE-003 resolved "Geyness" as the vendor name for the Genesys platform, so the only identifier that could plausibly be meant is GenesysInteractions.ConversationId — and no Genesys table exists in the merged schema, the module is out of this increment's scope, and a phone-intake ticket created without a Genesys interaction would have no such value regardless. Inventing a reference number the customer could quote back to an agent who cannot look it up would be worse than omitting it. A decision is required on what this field actually is.
RequestSummary and ticket status are omitted. They appear in this increment's brief gated on "if disclosure is allowed" / "only if approved", and no merged document grants either approval. Both are one small change away once granted.
What ships is the uncontested intersection: ticket number, creation timestamp, assigned department, and the expected first-response time. No internal note, audit record, assignee, escalation level or authorization information appears anywhere — a customer-facing message carries only what the customer is entitled to see.
UTC, labelled as such (NFR-UAE-01 — the system stores and reasons in UTC). Rendering into Asia/Dubai local time for the customer would read better, but no merged document specifies a customer-facing display zone or format, and silently shifting a contractual "expected response time" by four hours is not a formatting choice to make unilaterally. Flagged rather than guessed.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.Notifications.Services.TicketAcknowledgementHandler
member.summary:
FR-NOT-01 / backlog S-18 — the automated acknowledgement email, consumed from the TicketCreated Outbox event.
This path never satisfies the First Response SLA. FR-SLA-05 and ISSUE-019 exist because an acknowledgement fires within seconds of creation and would otherwise "satisfy" every first-response target automatically, making the KPI meaningless as a measure of service. Nothing here calls Ticket.RecordFirstHumanResponse, writes FirstHumanResponseAtUtc, touches SlaState, or reaches SlaBreachProcessor — a successful send writes exactly one ticket field, AcknowledgementSentAtUtc, which is a different column read by different code. The separation is structural, not a convention a future edit could quietly break: this class holds no reference to any service that could record a first response.
Idempotent, as ADR-0013 requires of every Outbox consumer. Delivery is at-least-once, so this handler can legitimately run twice for one event. Three independent guards stop that becoming two emails: Ticket.AcknowledgementSentAtUtc is write-once and short-circuits before anything is sent; the Notifications row is found rather than recreated, and a Sent one is terminal; and a unique index on (OutboxMessageId, NotificationType) makes a genuine race between two attempts a constraint violation rather than two delivery rows.
The residual at-least-once window is real and not claimed away. If the process dies after the provider accepts the message but before the commit that records it, a later attempt resends. Closing that would mean recording the send before making it, which turns a duplicate into a lost acknowledgement — the worse failure for a customer-facing receipt. The window is one local database write wide and is stated here rather than hidden.
Adds to the caller's unit of work; never saves and never sends inside a transaction. The dispatcher commits once per message, after the provider call has returned — holding a database transaction open across a network call would pin locks for the provider's latency.

member.name: T:TigerCS.Application.Modules.SlaAndEscalation.Abstractions.ISlaDeadlineScheduler
member.summary:
ADR-0015 / SLA-Architecture.md §13 — the primary breach-detection mechanism: a scheduled (delayed) background job enqueued per due timestamp at the moment it is computed, so the check fires at the exact due moment rather than waiting for a poll.
Abstracted here so the application layer never references Hangfire directly (Module-Design.md's dependency rules) and so the correctness of breach detection can be tested without a scheduler at all — the work a fired job performs lives in SlaBreachDetectionAppService, which is a plain service with no scheduling concern of its own.
Scheduling is an optimisation, never the guarantee. SLA-Architecture.md §14's recurring sweep independently re-scans due deadlines, so a job lost to a deploy or restart — or never enqueued at all, which is what the no-op implementation does — still results in the breach being detected. Both paths converge on the same idempotency key (§15), so whichever runs second changes nothing.

member.summary: Thrown by when persisting a VerificationSession consumption loses an optimistic-concurrency race — two concurrent ticket-creation requests both read the same Confirmed session before either committed, both passed the in-memory Consume() check, and only one write can win (MVP-ERD.md §2.24's single-use invariant, enforced here at the database level via a concurrency token on VerificationSessions.Status — see TigerCsDbContext's supplemental configuration). member.summary: The active SLA row for this exact (request type, priority) pair, or null when none is configured. No fallback is invented here: how an unconfigured pair relates to the existing per-priority SlaPolicy defaults is a phase-4 calculation decision recorded in docs/Workflow-SLA-Configuration-Phase1.md, and callers must treat null as "not configured", not as "no SLA".
